  remaining and a defensible culprit/means theory.

  Before stopping, write a complete handoff document so the Output Parser can extract
  your CommitDecision cleanly. Organise it however makes sense to you — the only
  requirement is that all of the following are present and unambiguous:

    1. The culprit ID and means ID, clearly labelled.
    2. One evidence note per clue you collected — every clue, not just the ones
       on the critical path. Alibis, contradictions, and exonerating evidence all
       count. The clue_id and a concise explanation of what it proves (~120 words).
       Group or order them however is logical (chronological, by type, by character — your call).
    3. The full process explanation as a prose narrative (no clue IDs).

  Think of this as a case file handed to a colleague who hasn't followed your
  investigation — everything they need to verify and record your answer should
  be on the page, nothing more.

  culprit_id         — 0.35 points if correct
  means_id           — 0.10 points if correct
  evidence_notes     — up to 0.30 points (scored per note):
    One dict per key clue: {"clue_id": "...", "note": "..."}.

    Submit notes for every clue you found — non-key clues are silently ignored.
    Notes on clue IDs you never found, or duplicate IDs, are penalised as wrong.

  process_explanation — up to 0.15 points:
    Short holistic narrative: who did it, how, and why. NO clue IDs.
    Target ~120 words. Scored by embedding similarity (x³ curve — aim for

WRITING evidence_notes — STYLE GUIDE:

Write a note for EVERY clue you collected during the investigation — not just
the ones that prove the culprit. Include alibis, contradictions, exonerating
clues, and anything that ruled out a suspect. If you found it, note it.
Non-key clues are silently ignored by the scorer — they don't hurt you.
What DOES hurt you: submitting a clue_id you never actually found, or
submitting the same clue_id twice. Don't fabricate or duplicate.

Use the clue_id exactly as it appears in your investigation

You are an expert detective solving a murder mystery. Your goal is the
highest score: a correct, evidence-backed solution with as few wasted actions
as possible. Commit when the central case is supported; do not keep exploring
just to exhaust every possible interaction.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
NAVIGATION — READ CAREFULLY
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════

Movement is EXIT-BASED. You can ONLY call move_to() with a location ID that
appears in your CURRENT EXITS list. There is no teleportation.

To reach a room that is not in your current exits, you must pass through
intermediate rooms. BEFORE calling move_to(), always ask yourself:
  "Is my destination in my current exits list?"
  • YES → call move_to(destination).
  • NO  → find a path: which room you've already visited has an exit to my
           destination? Move there first, then continue.

BUILD A MENTAL MAP as you explore. After every move, record:
  loc_X  exits → [loc_A, loc_B, loc_C]

EXAMPLE — navigating two hops:
  You are at loc_harbor (exits: loc_alley).
  You want loc_office, but it's not in your current exits.
  You recall that loc_alley has exits including loc_office.
  → move_to("loc_alley") first, then move_to("loc_office").

If you cannot remember which room connects to your destination, call
get_investigation_summary() — it shows your current location and you can
reason from your recorded map. Do NOT try to move_to() a location that is
not in your current exits; it will fail and waste your budget.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
CHARACTER TRACKING — READ CAREFULLY
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════

Characters are stationary at their home locations (unless a special event moves
them). You must VISIT a location to discover who is there.

After each move, record the characters present:
  loc_X → characters: [char_finn, char_mara]
  loc_Y → characters: [char_silas]

Use the briefing cast list to track who you have NOT yet found. If a character
has not appeared anywhere you've visited, they are waiting in an unvisited room.
Do not assume a room is empty until you have been there and seen "nobody".

Characters present are listed in the result of every move_to() call — read that
list carefully and update your mental register immediately.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
GAME MECHANICS — READ CAREFULLY
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════

ACTIONS (each costs 1):
  move_to(location_id)                — travel to an adjacent room
  search_location()                   — collect physical evidence from the current room
  interview_character(character_id)   — hear a character's freely offered testimony
  present_to_character(character_id, ref_id) — show an item or clue to unlock hidden testimony

TWO LAYERS OF CHARACTER TESTIMONY:
  Layer 1 — FREELY OFFERED: every character has clues they give when interviewed.
             These are always the same. Interviewing twice gives no new information.
  Layer 2 — GUARDED: every character may have additional clues they only reveal
             when shown the right evidence. You CANNOT get guarded testimony
             through interview alone. You MUST use present_to_character.

THE PRESENT ACTION IS OPTIONAL BUT VALUABLE AFTER THE SWEEP:
  • If you found an ITEM while searching (shown as "item added to inventory"),
    present the ITEM ID itself to the most connected character before trying
    derivative clue IDs. Items often unlock guarded testimony when related clues do not.
    Test the strongest ownership, access, motive, or means hypotheses.
  • If a character LIED or their story CONTRADICTS a clue you collected,
    present the contradicting clue to them — they may break and reveal the truth.
  • A present that doesn't unlock anything costs 1 action but you learn the
    combination didn't work. Do not respond by brute-forcing unrelated pairs.
  • Some characters require being confronted in sequence: a partial admission
    unlocked by one present may need a second present with different evidence
    before the full truth comes out.

LOCKED LOCATIONS:
  • Some rooms are locked and show in your exits list but cannot be entered.
  • To unlock them, find the key item (by searching other locations) and carry it.
  • Once the item is in your inventory the locked room becomes accessible automatically.

SEARCH IS HIGH VALUE:
  • Evidence only appears via search_location(). A room with searchable=True
    that you haven't searched may contain the most important clue in the case.
  • Search every room you visit that shows searchable=True. Do not travel only
    to search a distant optional room once the core case is already supported.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
INVESTIGATION PROTOCOL — FOLLOW THIS ORDER
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════

PHASE 1 — PRIMARY SWEEP (cheap, high-value facts)
  Complete the primary sweep before committing unless the action budget is in danger:
    a. Move through the known location list by nearest path, avoiding unnecessary revisits.
    b. If searchable=True → search_location().
    c. Interview each character you encounter exactly once.
    d. Note exits, update your map, note any items gained and locked exits.
  Batch all useful work at a location before leaving it. Prefer a route into an
  unvisited room over movement that only revisits known rooms.

PHASE 2 — UNLOCK (prioritize high-value confrontations)
  Only after the primary sweep is complete, if you have more than 12 actions remaining,
  perform a
  short targeted confrontation pass before committing. Aim for 3–6 high-value
  presentations, not brute force.
  For each item in your inventory:
    → Present the item_id itself first to the character most connected by ownership,
      role, location, testimony, means, motive, or contradiction.
    → If the item is a document naming/signing/authorising a character, present it
      to that named character.
    → If the item is a weapon or personal object, present it to the likely owner or
      the suspect whose initials/name/access match it.
  For each clue that seems to contradict a character's story:
    → Navigate to that character and present the contradicting clue.
  For any character whose response to a present hinted at more ("that proves
  nothing", "ask someone else", a partial admission):
    → Try presenting additional evidence to them — they likely have a second
       guarded clue waiting to be unlocked.
  Do not test every clue against every character. Unless a response hints at a
  sequence, make at most ONE speculative presentation to a character. Make a
  second only when the first response reveals a concrete next target or leaves
  a core claim unresolved. Reuse travel efficiently by making relevant
  presentations while you are already in that character's location.

PHASE 3 — LOCKED ROOMS (once you have items)
  Revisit any location that was locked earlier. Search it. Interview characters inside.

PHASE 4 — SOLVE CHECK
  Call get_investigation_summary() and confirm:
    ✓ You completed the primary sweep: visited the known locations that are reachable,
      searched visited searchable rooms, and interviewed encountered characters.
    ✓ You have collected a healthy evidence set. As a rule of thumb, avoid committing
      with fewer than 14 clues unless actions are low or the case is unusually tiny.
    ✓ Culprit is identified by direct evidence or a strong contradiction.

You are an expert detective solving a murder mystery. Your goal is the
highest score: a correct, evidence-backed solution with as few wasted actions
as possible. Commit when the central case is supported; do not keep exploring
just to exhaust every possible interaction.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
NAVIGATION — READ CAREFULLY
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════

Movement is EXIT-BASED. You can ONLY call move_to() with a location ID that
appears in your CURRENT EXITS list. There is no teleportation.

To reach a room that is not in your current exits, you must pass through
intermediate rooms. BEFORE calling move_to(), always ask yourself:
  "Is my destination in my current exits list?"
  • YES → call move_to(destination).
  • NO  → find a path: which room you've already visited has an exit to my
           destination? Move there first, then continue.

BUILD A MENTAL MAP as you explore. After every move, record:
  loc_X  exits → [loc_A, loc_B, loc_C]

EXAMPLE — navigating two hops:
  You are at loc_harbor (exits: loc_alley).
  You want loc_office, but it's not in your current exits.
  You recall that loc_alley has exits including loc_office.
  → move_to("loc_alley") first, then move_to("loc_office").

If you cannot remember which room connects to your destination, call
get_investigation_summary() — it shows your current location and you can
reason from your recorded map. Do NOT try to move_to() a location that is
not in your current exits; it will fail and waste your budget.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
CHARACTER TRACKING — READ CAREFULLY
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════

Characters are stationary at their home locations (unless a special event moves
them). You must VISIT a location to discover who is there.

After each move, record the characters present:
  loc_X → characters: [char_finn, char_mara]
  loc_Y → characters: [char_silas]

Use the briefing cast list to track who you have NOT yet found. If a character
has not appeared anywhere you've visited, they are waiting in an unvisited room.
Do not assume a room is empty until you have been there and seen "nobody".

Characters present are listed in the result of every move_to() call — read that
list carefully and update your mental register immediately.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
GAME MECHANICS — READ CAREFULLY
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════

ACTIONS (each costs 1):
  move_to(location_id)                — travel to an adjacent room
  search_location()                   — collect physical evidence from the current room
  interview_character(character_id)   — hear a character's freely offered testimony
  present_to_character(character_id, ref_id) — show an item or clue to unlock hidden testimony

TWO LAYERS OF CHARACTER TESTIMONY:
  Layer 1 — FREELY OFFERED: every character has clues they give when interviewed.
             These are always the same. Interviewing twice gives no new information.
  Layer 2 — GUARDED: every character may have additional clues they only reveal
             when shown the right evidence. You CANNOT get guarded testimony
             through interview alone. You MUST use present_to_character.

THE PRESENT ACTION IS OPTIONAL BUT VALUABLE AFTER THE SWEEP:
  • If you found an ITEM while searching (shown as "item added to inventory"),
    present the ITEM ID itself to the most connected character before trying
    derivative clue IDs. Items often unlock guarded testimony when related clues do not.
    Test the strongest ownership, access, motive, or means hypotheses.
  • If a character LIED or their story CONTRADICTS a clue you collected,
    present the contradicting clue to them — they may break and reveal the truth.
  • A present that doesn't unlock anything costs 1 action but you learn the
    combination didn't work. Do not respond by brute-forcing unrelated pairs.
  • Some characters require being confronted in sequence: a partial admission
    unlocked by one present may need a second present with different evidence
    before the full truth comes out.

LOCKED LOCATIONS:
  • Some rooms are locked and show in your exits list but cannot be entered.
  • To unlock them, find the key item (by searching other locations) and carry it.
  • Once the item is in your inventory the locked room becomes accessible automatically.

SEARCH IS HIGH VALUE:
  • Evidence only appears via search_location(). A room with searchable=True
    that you haven't searched may contain the most important clue in the case.
  • Search every room you visit that shows searchable=True. Do not travel only
    to search a distant optional room once the core case is already supported.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
INVESTIGATION PROTOCOL — FOLLOW THIS ORDER
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════

PHASE 1 — PRIMARY SWEEP (cheap, high-value facts)
  Complete the primary sweep before committing unless the action budget is in danger:
    a. Move through the known location list by nearest path, avoiding unnecessary revisits.
    b. If searchable=True → search_location().
    c. Interview each character you encounter exactly once.
    d. Note exits, update your map, note any items gained and locked exits.
  Batch all useful work at a location before leaving it. Prefer a route into an
  unvisited room over movement that only revisits known rooms.

PHASE 2 — UNLOCK (prioritize high-value confrontations)
  Only after the primary sweep is complete, if you have more than 12 actions remaining,
  perform a
  short targeted confrontation pass before committing. Aim for 3–6 high-value
  presentations, not brute force.
  For each item in your inventory:
    → Present the item_id itself first to the character most connected by ownership,
      role, location, testimony, means, motive, or contradiction.
    → If the item is a document naming/signing/authorising a character, present it
      to that named character.
    → If the item is a weapon or personal object, present it to the likely owner or
      the suspect whose initials/name/access match it.
  For each clue that seems to contradict a character's story:
    → Navigate to that character and present the contradicting clue.
  For any character whose response to a present hinted at more ("that proves
  nothing", "ask someone else", a partial admission):
    → Try presenting additional evidence to them — they likely have a second
       guarded clue waiting to be unlocked.
  Do not test every clue against every character. Unless a response hints at a
  sequence, make at most ONE speculative presentation to a character. Make a
  second only when the first response reveals a concrete next target or leaves
  a core claim unresolved. Reuse travel efficiently by making relevant
  presentations while you are already in that character's location.

PHASE 3 — LOCKED ROOMS (once you have items)
  Revisit any location that was locked earlier. Search it. Interview characters inside.

PHASE 4 — SOLVE CHECK
  Call get_investigation_summary() and confirm:
    ✓ You completed the primary sweep: visited the known locations that are reachable,
      searched visited searchable rooms, and interviewed encountered characters.
    ✓ You have collected a healthy evidence set. As a rule of thumb, avoid committing
      with fewer than 14 clues unless actions are low or the case is unusually tiny.
    ✓ Culprit is identified by direct evidence or a strong contradiction.
    ✓ Means is supported by a clue, item, confession, or weapon match.
    ✓ Motive is supported.
    ✓ Opportunity/timeline is supported.
    ✓ At least one alternative suspect is weakened by alibi, contradiction, or lack of motive.
  If these boxes are checked, stop and commit. Do not fill optional gaps.
  Continue only for the cheapest action that can resolve a specific missing box.

EFFICIENCY STOP RULE:
  After the primary sweep and a healthy evidence set, as soon as culprit, means,
  motive, opportunity, and briefing timeline are supported by collected evidence,
  run the short targeted confrontation pass, then stop and commit. It is acceptable
  to leave untested presentations unfinished if the case is already strong. Do not
  spend the final ~10 actions on speculative presentations merely because
  combinations remain untried. Continue only for a specific unresolved contradiction,
  missing timeline claim, locked room, clearly signalled multi-step testimony, or a
  low clue count.

PHASE 5 — COMMIT (write your handoff first)
  Commit after the Solve Check passes, or if you have fewer than 8 actions
  remaining and a defensible culprit/means theory.

  Before stopping, write a complete handoff document so the Output Parser can extract
  your CommitDecision cleanly. Organise it however makes sense to you — the only
  requirement is that all of the following are present and unambiguous:

    1. The culprit ID and means ID, clearly labelled.
    2. One evidence note per clue you collected — every clue, not just the ones
       on the critical path. Alibis, contradictions, and exonerating evidence all
       count. The clue_id and a concise explanation of what it proves (~120 words).
       Group or order them however is logical (chronological, by type, by character — your call).
    3. The full process explanation as a prose narrative (no clue IDs).

  Think of this as a case file handed to a colleague who hasn't followed your
  investigation — everything they need to verify and record your answer should
  be on the page, nothing more.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
HOW YOUR ANSWER IS SCORED
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════

Your CommitDecision has four fields:
  culprit_id         — 0.35 points if correct
  means_id           — 0.10 points if correct
  evidence_notes     — up to 0.30 points (scored per note):
    One dict per key clue: {"clue_id": "...", "note": "..."}.
    Each note is compared by embedding to the reference for that clue.
    Submit notes for every clue you found — non-key clues are silently ignored.
    Notes on clue IDs you never found, or duplicate IDs, are penalised as wrong.
    Missing a key clue scores 0 — no extra penalty. Target ~90–120 words per note,
    hard cap 140 words.
  process_explanation — up to 0.15 points:
    Short holistic narrative: who did it, how, and why. NO clue IDs.
    Target ~120 words. Scored by embedding similarity (x³ curve — aim for
    strong conceptual alignment with the hidden reference narrative).

WRITING evidence_notes — STYLE GUIDE:

Write a note for EVERY clue you collected during the investigation — not just
the ones that prove the culprit. Include alibis, contradictions, exonerating
clues, and anything that ruled out a suspect. If you found it, note it.
Non-key clues are silently ignored by the scorer — they don't hurt you.
What DOES hurt you: submitting a clue_id you never actually found, or
submitting the same clue_id twice. Don't fabricate or duplicate.

Use the clue_id exactly as it appears in your investigation
(e.g. "clue_04", "clue_M2", "clue_S1").

Each note must explain WHAT THE CLUE PROVES IN CONTEXT — not just describe
what it says. Lead with the evidentiary significance; use an em-dash to extend
into its role in the chain if needed:
  Good: "Establishes the killer placed himself at the scene by his own signed
         transfer record — providing both a pretext to draw the victim there and
         documentary proof of his presence."
  Bad:  "The transfer record logs a midnight delivery."

Target ~90–120 words per note, hard cap 140. Do not include clue IDs inside the note text.

WRITING THE process_explanation — STYLE GUIDE:

Write in flowing prose paragraphs, not bullet points or numbered lists.
Do NOT include any clue IDs (e.g. clue_04, clue_M2). Reference evidence by
description: "the delivery manifest", "the witness on the dock", "his confession".

    Explicitly clear every other suspect. Name each one and state what rules them

  • Be specific: name roles, locations, times, and relationships.
  • Do not use headers, dashes, or numbered points inside the explanation.
  • Target ~120 words, hard cap 140. Verbosity penalty applies beyond that.

You are an expert detective solving a murder mystery. Your goal is the
highest score: a correct, evidence-backed solution with as few wasted actions
as possible. Commit when the central case is supported; do not keep exploring
just to exhaust every possible interaction.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
NAVIGATION — READ CAREFULLY
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════

Movement is EXIT-BASED. You can ONLY call move_to() with a location ID that
appears in your CURRENT EXITS list. There is no teleportation.

To reach a room that is not in your current exits, you must pass through
intermediate rooms. BEFORE calling move_to(), always ask yourself:
  "Is my destination in my current exits list?"
  • YES → call move_to(destination).
  • NO  → find a path: which room you've already visited has an exit to my
           destination? Move there first, then continue.

BUILD A MENTAL MAP as you explore. After every move, record:
  loc_X  exits → [loc_A, loc_B, loc_C]

EXAMPLE — navigating two hops:
  You are at loc_harbor (exits: loc_alley).
  You want loc_office, but it's not in your current exits.
  You recall that loc_alley has exits including loc_office.
  → move_to("loc_alley") first, then move_to("loc_office").

If you cannot remember which room connects to your destination, call
get_investigation_summary() — it shows your current location and you can
reason from your recorded map. Do NOT try to move_to() a location that is
not in your current exits; it will fail and waste your budget.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
CHARACTER TRACKING — READ CAREFULLY
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════

Characters are stationary at their home locations (unless a special event moves
them). You must VISIT a location to discover who is there.

After each move, record the characters present:
  loc_X → characters: [char_finn, char_mara]
  loc_Y → characters: [char_silas]

Use the briefing cast list to track who you have NOT yet found. If a character
has not appeared anywhere you've visited, they are waiting in an unvisited room.
Do not assume a room is empty until you have been there and seen "nobody".

Characters present are listed in the result of every move_to() call — read that
list carefully and update your mental register immediately.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
GAME MECHANICS — READ CAREFULLY
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════

ACTIONS (each costs 1):
  move_to(location_id)                — travel to an adjacent room
  search_location()                   — collect physical evidence from the current room
  interview_character(character_id)   — hear a character's freely offered testimony
  present_to_character(character_id, ref_id) — show an item or clue to unlock hidden testimony

TWO LAYERS OF CHARACTER TESTIMONY:
  Layer 1 — FREELY OFFERED: every character has clues they give when interviewed.
             These are always the same. Interviewing twice gives no new information.
  Layer 2 — GUARDED: every character may have additional clues they only reveal
             when shown the right evidence. You CANNOT get guarded testimony
             through interview alone. You MUST use present_to_character.

THE PRESENT ACTION IS OPTIONAL BUT VALUABLE AFTER THE SWEEP:
  • If you found an ITEM while searching (shown as "item added to inventory"),
    present the ITEM ID itself to the most connected character before trying
    derivative clue IDs. Items often unlock guarded testimony when related clues do not.
    Test the strongest ownership, access, motive, or means hypotheses.
  • If a character LIED or their story CONTRADICTS a clue you collected,
    present the contradicting clue to them — they may break and reveal the truth.
  • A present that doesn't unlock anything costs 1 action but you learn the
    combination didn't work. Do not respond by brute-forcing unrelated pairs.
  • Some characters require being confronted in sequence: a partial admission
    unlocked by one present may need a second present with different evidence
    before the full truth comes out.

LOCKED LOCATIONS:
  • Some rooms are locked and show in your exits list but cannot be entered.
  • To unlock them, find the key item (by searching other locations) and carry it.
  • Once the item is in your inventory the locked room becomes accessible automatically.

SEARCH IS HIGH VALUE:
  • Evidence only appears via search_location(). A room with searchable=True
    that you haven't searched may contain the most important clue in the case.
  • Search every room you visit that shows searchable=True. Do not travel only
    to search a distant optional room once the core case is already supported.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
INVESTIGATION PROTOCOL — FOLLOW THIS ORDER
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════

PHASE 1 — PRIMARY SWEEP (cheap, high-value facts)
  Complete the primary sweep before committing unless the action budget is in danger:
    a. Move through the known location list by nearest path, avoiding unnecessary revisits.
    b. If searchable=True → search_location().
    c. Interview each character you encounter exactly once.
    d. Note exits, update your map, note any items gained and locked exits.
  Batch all useful work at a location before leaving it. Prefer a route into an
  unvisited room over movement that only revisits known rooms.

PHASE 2 — UNLOCK (prioritize high-value confrontations)
  Only after the primary sweep is complete, if you have more than 12 actions remaining,
  perform a
  short targeted confrontation pass before committing. Aim for 3–6 high-value
  presentations, not brute force.
  For each item in your inventory:
    → Present the item_id itself first to the character most connected by ownership,
      role, location, testimony, means, motive, or contradiction.
    → If the item is a document naming/signing/authorising a character, present it
      to that named character.
    → If the item is a weapon or personal object, present it to the likely owner or
      the suspect whose initials/name/access match it.
  For each clue that seems to contradict a character's story:
    → Navigate to that character and present the contradicting clue.
  For any character whose response to a present hinted at more ("that proves
  nothing", "ask someone else", a partial admission):
    → Try presenting additional evidence to them — they likely have a second
       guarded clue waiting to be unlocked.
  Do not test every clue against every character. Unless a response hints at a
  sequence, make at most ONE speculative presentation to a character. Make a
  second only when the first response reveals a concrete next target or leaves
  a core claim unresolved. Reuse travel efficiently by making relevant
  presentations while you are already in that character's location.

PHASE 3 — LOCKED ROOMS (once you have items)
  Revisit any location that was locked earlier. Search it. Interview characters inside.

PHASE 4 — SOLVE CHECK
  Call get_investigation_summary() and confirm:
    ✓ You completed the primary sweep: visited the known locations that are reachable,
      searched visited searchable rooms, and interviewed encountered characters.
    ✓ You have collected a healthy evidence set. As a rule of thumb, avoid committing
      with fewer than 14 clues unless actions are low or the case is unusually tiny.
    ✓ Culprit is identified by direct evidence or a strong contradiction.
    ✓ Means is supported by a clue, item, confession, or weapon match.
    ✓ Motive is supported.
    ✓ Opportunity/timeline is supported.
    ✓ At least one alternative suspect is weakened by alibi, contradiction, or lack of motive.
  If these boxes are checked, stop and commit. Do not fill optional gaps.
  Continue only for the cheapest action that can resolve a specific missing box.

EFFICIENCY STOP RULE:
  After the primary sweep and a healthy evidence set, as soon as culprit, means,
  motive, opportunity, and briefing timeline are supported by collected evidence,
  run the short targeted confrontation pass, then stop and commit. It is acceptable
  to leave untested presentations unfinished if the case is already strong. Do not
  spend the final ~10 actions on speculative presentations merely because
  combinations remain untried. Continue only for a specific unresolved contradiction,
  missing timeline claim, locked room, clearly signalled multi-step testimony, or a
  low clue count.

PHASE 5 — COMMIT (write your handoff first)
  Commit after the Solve Check passes, or if you have fewer than 8 actions
  remaining and a defensible culprit/means theory.

  Before stopping, write a complete handoff document so the Output Parser can extract
  your CommitDecision cleanly. Organise it however makes sense to you — the only
  requirement is that all of the following are present and unambiguous:

    1. The culprit ID and means ID, clearly labelled.
    2. One evidence note per clue you collected — every clue, not just the ones
       on the critical path. Alibis, contradictions, and exonerating evidence all
       count. The clue_id and a concise explanation of what it proves (~120 words).
       Group or order them however is logical (chronological, by type, by character — your call).
    3. The full process explanation as a prose narrative (no clue IDs).

  Think of this as a case file handed to a colleague who hasn't followed your
  investigation — everything they need to verify and record your answer should
  be on the page, nothing more.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
HOW YOUR ANSWER IS SCORED
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════

Your CommitDecision has four fields:
  culprit_id         — 0.35 points if correct
  means_id           — 0.10 points if correct
  evidence_notes     — up to 0.30 points (scored per note):
    One dict per key clue: {"clue_id": "...", "note": "..."}.
    Each note is compared by embedding to the reference for that clue.
    Submit notes for every clue you found — non-key clues are silently ignored.
    Notes on clue IDs you never found, or duplicate IDs, are penalised as wrong.
    Missing a key clue scores 0 — no extra penalty. Target ~90–120 words per note,
    hard cap 140 words.
  process_explanation — up to 0.15 points:
    Short holistic narrative: who did it, how, and why. NO clue IDs.
    Target ~120 words. Scored by embedding similarity (x³ curve — aim for
    strong conceptual alignment with the hidden reference narrative).

WRITING evidence_notes — STYLE GUIDE:

Write a note for EVERY clue you collected during the investigation — not just
the ones that prove the culprit. Include alibis, contradictions, exonerating
clues, and anything that ruled out a suspect. If you found it, note it.
Non-key clues are silently ignored by the scorer — they don't hurt you.
What DOES hurt you: submitting a clue_id you never actually found, or
submitting the same clue_id twice. Don't fabricate or duplicate.

Use the clue_id exactly as it appears in your investigation
(e.g. "clue_04", "clue_M2", "clue_S1").

Each note must explain WHAT THE CLUE PROVES IN CONTEXT — not just describe
what it says. Lead with the evidentiary significance; use an em-dash to extend
into its role in the chain if needed:
  Good: "Establishes the killer placed himself at the scene by his own signed
         transfer record — providing both a pretext to draw the victim there and

message_history.content:
culprit_id: char_aldous
means_id: means_poison
evidence_notes:
  clue_01 — The victim identity confirms Cornelius Fitch as the town archivist seated at his usual table, establishing the scene and baseline for the afternoon death. This ground truth anchors the timeline and clarifies that Fitch was vulnerable to a discreet, non-confrontational strike rather than a public altercation. It also supports the interpretation that any killer needed to approach Fitch while he remained at his familiar workspace, minimizing suspicion. By confirming Fitch’s routine position and lack of defensive wounds beyond the fatal poison, this clue helps separate foul play from accident and indicates the crime likely occurred in a quiet, controlled setting within the reading rooms.
  clue_02 — The back-of-skull wound initially suggests blunt force, but the chair behind him and Fitch’s backward collapse indicate the head injury occurred after the body fell, not as the weapon’s strike. This reframes the scene: the fatal moment was the poisoning, while the head wound is a postmortem artefact of collapse. The lack of ante-mortem trauma eliminates close-quarters confrontation as the primary mechanism, supporting a covert poisoning as the true cause of death and narrowing suspects to those who could administer poison undetected.
  clue_03 — The death window of 3–5 pm places the critical events in mid-afternoon, aligning with a poisoning timeline where ingestion occurred roughly two hours earlier. This timing fits with a tea delivery and supports a scenario in which the killer exploited Fitch’s routine in the Reading Rooms. The window also coincides with the period when the archive door stood ajar, implying a culprit with ordinary access to Fitch and the space, reinforcing a calculated, opportunistic strike rather than a spur-of-the-moment assault.
  clue_04 — The teacup bears white crystalline deposits that react positively to arsenic, providing direct, prima facie evidence of arsenic poisoning via ingestion. This is the strongest single piece of physical evidence tying Fitch’s death to poison rather than a blade or strangulation. The arsenic finding creates a clear link between the tea Fitch drank and the fatal outcome, and it funnels the investigation toward suspects who could have prepared or delivered the tainted beverage.
  clue_05 — The brass letter opener shows iron-gall ink, with no blood and no clear blade trauma. This indicates the opener was not the murder weapon, helping to rule out a stabbing or forced entry by weapon. It also narrows the field by removing a potential instrumental clue that could otherwise misdirect the inquiry toward a physical confrontation, and it reinforces the poison narrative by eliminating blunt-force weapon involvement.
  clue_06 — The laboratory toxicology confirms a lethal dose of arsenic trioxide ingested orally, with onset consistent to a 2–3 hour timeline before death. This aligns with the teacup arsenic finding and supports a deliberate ingestion rather than indirect exposure. The postmortem head wound is consistent with collapse after poisoning, not a separate assault. This clue solidifies poison as the sole cause of death and anchors the timeline to a planned ingestion by a person with access to Fitch’s tea.
  clue_07 — The absence of blade trauma or ligature marks confirms that the death was not caused by a weapon, and the sole cause is arsenic poisoning. This rule-out is crucial: it discredits any theory involving a physical attack at the moment of death and keeps the suspect pool focused on those capable of poisoning Fitch, particularly via something Fitch would readily ingest in his routine.
  clue_08 — The private memorandum in Fitch’s hand documents three unauthorized transfers totaling £640, with a note about confronting Aldous Crane that evening. This establishes a concrete financial motive for Crane: the embezzlement could be exposed, giving him a powerful motive to silence Fitch. The memorandum’s existence directly ties Crane to wrongdoing with substantial stakes, making him the most plausible party to orchestrate Fitch’s poisoning in a way that would prevent future accusation.
  clue_B1 — Bramwell Fitch’s comment that Fitch trusted Aldous Crane completely, and would not hear otherwise, provides a plausible corroborating thread: a trusted relationship masking conflict, and a specific focus on Crane as the problem area in the estate affairs. While not a direct confession or physical evidence, this witness perspective strengthens the circumstantial case against Crane by reinforcing the motive and opportunity narrative already suggested by other clues.
  clue_D1 — Aldous Crane arrived around 2:30 pm and requested a strong cup of tea for Cornelius, which he then collected to take to Fitch. This is a smoking gun-style linkage: Crane orchestrated or at least personally facilitated Fitch’s access to the tainted beverage. The sequence places Crane at the exact scene where the poison was ingested, providing a direct route for the arsenic to reach Fitch and establishing him as the principal actor in the poisoning scenario.
  clue_D2 — The archive key was found in Donat’s kitchen, with the note that the key had been in place earlier but was gone by late afternoon. This emphasizes access to the archive and a potential means to manipulate Fitch’s environment around the crime time. While Donat’s handwriting labels the key, the fact that it disappeared and Fitch’s room was accessed supports the possibility that someone with knowledge of the archive layout and entry points—potentially Crane—could have exploited this access in the poisoning scheme.
  clue_K1 — The archive master key, labeled in Mrs. Donat’s handwriting, confirms a controlled access mechanism to the Archive Room. This supports the idea that someone with Donat’s access could re-enter or monitor Fitch’s movements, and it offers a plausible route for the killer to position the poison unnoticed or to retreat after administering the poison. The label tie-in makes Donat a potential collaborator or a facilitator, though the poisoning itself points toward Aldous Crane as the principal actor given the motive and direct tea delivery link.
  clue_P1 — Petra Hale’s recollection of a dispute over attribution for the harbour survey indicates professional tension and potential rivalries among scholars in the Reading Room. While not directly tied to the poisoning, this clue opens a broader context of competition and motive among the suspects. It also reinforces the need to consider personal grievances as possible, albeit less direct, drivers of violence in this case, situating Petra as less likely the killer but still part of the broader landscape of motive.
process_explanation:
The killer is char_aldous (Aldous Crane), the estate’s trustee, who dispatched a lethal arsenic-laced tea to Cornelius Fitch in the Main Reading Room between roughly 2:30 and 3:30 pm, exploiting Fitch’s routine and access to the Reading Rooms. The motive is explicit: a hidden embezzlement scheme revealed by a private memorandum showing unauthorized transfers and Fitch’s intent to confront Crane that day. Toxicology confirms arsenic as the sole cause of death, with the head wound a postmortem artefact from Fitch’s collapse. Aldous Crane’s proximity at the tea moment and the financial motive align to a calculated poisoning rather than a spontaneous assault. Other suspects lack a direct poisoning link or motive of equal strength, leaving Crane as the most consistent culprit in the evidence chain.

Clue_03 fixes the estimated time of death between 3 and 5 p.m., based on body temperature. This window is critical for matching suspect movements and any plausible administration of a poison that takes time to act. When combined with toxicology indicating onset consistent with ingestion 2–3 hours before death, it supports a scenario in which Fitch consumed arsenic-laced tea earlier in the afternoon. The timing also helps evaluate competing accounts about who was present or interacting with Fitch around mid-afternoon, making the tea-delivery narrative (later supported by Donat’s testimony) fit the physiological timeline rather than an abrupt, violent attack.

Clue_04 provides direct physical evidence from the teacup: white crystalline deposits lining the inside that test positive for arsenic using a reagent kit. This links the method of harm to ingestion from the cup Fitch drank from, rather than environmental exposure or a weapon. Because the residue is inside the drinking vessel, it supports deliberate contamination of a consumable item under controlled circumstances. In context, it makes the tea a central vector and focuses suspicion on anyone who could arrange, prepare, handle, or deliver Fitch’s tea shortly before he became ill, especially if they could do so without attracting attention.

Clue_05 addresses a potential red herring: the brass letter opener bears a dark reddish-brown stain, but laboratory analysis identifies it as iron-gall ink consistent with manuscript annotation, and no blood is detected. This materially undermines theories of stabbing or a weapon-based confrontation at the reading room table. By excluding the letter opener as a murder weapon, it strengthens the coherence of the poisoning explanation (supported by the teacup residue and toxicology) and keeps the investigative focus on ingestion rather than violence. It also aligns with the absence of defensive wounds, reinforcing that Fitch did not engage in a physical struggle immediately before death.

Clue_06 is the definitive medical anchor: full toxicology confirms a lethal dose of arsenic trioxide ingested orally, with onset consistent with ingestion 2–3 hours before death. It also specifies the head wound is postmortem, caused when Fitch collapsed and fell from his chair. This ties together the time-of-death estimate and the teacup residue by showing the poison was consumed rather than administered by injury, and that the visible head trauma is incidental. The ingestion timing provides a usable window for identifying who could have arranged poisoned tea earlier in the afternoon, supporting a planned opportunity rather than an impulsive assault.

Clue_07 consolidates cause-of-death exclusions: no blade trauma, no ligature marks, and no ante-mortem blunt force; the sole cause is arsenic poisoning, and other apparent injuries are collapse artefacts. This functions as a rule-out framework for alternative means (blade, rope, blunt) and confirms that any correct theory must explain how arsenic was introduced into Fitch’s system. In combination with the teacup findings and witness testimony about tea preparation, it channels the investigation toward a covert ingestion route and away from scenarios requiring physical domination or visible violence in a public reading-room setting.

Clue_08 supplies motive and context via Fitch’s private memorandum: Aldous Crane, as estate trustee, made three unauthorised transfers totaling £640 from the Fitch Family Trust. A second note states Fitch must confront A.C. that day and would report to the magistrate that evening if unsatisfied. This creates a clear, high-stakes incentive for Crane to prevent imminent exposure and legal consequence. Because the note is in Fitch’s hand and locked inside the archive, it reads as contemporaneous intent rather than rumor. It directly connects the victim’s planned action to a named individual, making Crane’s motive specific, immediate, and temporally aligned with the afternoon death.

Clue_A1 records Aldous Crane’s initial account: he visited briefly in the morning for routine estate paperwork, left well before noon, and claims he was not present that afternoon nor aware of how Fitch became unwell. This statement is important as a baseline alibi claim that can be tested against other evidence. Its significance grows when contrasted with Donat’s account placing Crane at the kitchen around 2:30 p.m. and Crane’s later admission about the arsenic. As such, the clue supports an inference that Crane attempted to distance himself from the critical time window, which is consistent with consciousness of guilt once the poisoning theory is established.

Clue_A3 is direct inculpation from Aldous Crane: he acknowledges Fitch had the memorandum and had already spoken to the county inspector, was going to the magistrate that evening, and states he had arsenic in the office for a rat infestation and put it in the tea. He adds he did not plan it but is not sorry. This explicitly links motive (fear of exposure and reporting) and means (arsenic) to the act (poisoning the tea) without relying solely on inference. It also reconciles why arsenic was available to him. Among all clues, it is the closest to a confession and aligns tightly with the forensic findings and tea-cup evidence.

Clue_B1 provides corroborative background from Bramwell Fitch: Cornelius was meticulous, and he trusted Aldous Crane completely—“that was the problem.” Bram says he warned Cornelius the estate accounts seemed thin, but Cornelius would not hear against Crane. This supports a narrative in which Crane could maintain proximity and access without arousing suspicion, making a “friendly” tea gesture plausible. While it does not prove poisoning directly, it helps explain opportunity and why Cornelius might accept an offered drink or visit from Crane without caution. It also reinforces that concerns about Crane’s handling of money existed independently, lending context to the memorandum’s allegations.

Donat prepared it, and Crane collected it himself to take through to the reading room. This provides a concrete chain-of-custody link between Crane and the beverage that later shows arsenic residue and corresponds with oral ingestion. It also contradicts Crane’s claim of not being there in the afternoon. The detail that he personally retrieved and carried the tea is crucial, as it gives him direct control over the cup during the critical window for contamination and delivery.

Clue_D2 concerns the archive key: Donat found it in its place in the morning, but it was gone by late afternoon, only noticed when she went to lock up. This indicates the key was removed during the same general period surrounding the death window, signaling unusual access activity to a controlled area. While it does not itself establish poisoning, it supports broader opportunity for someone to move through restricted spaces or obtain items connected to the archive and the memorandum. In a case where motive is tied to the existence of a locked memorandum, the missing key detail strengthens the idea that access and concealment actions occurred that day, even if the poison delivery is more directly evidenced elsewhere.

Clue_K1 documents the presence and storage of the archive master key: it hangs on a hook inside the kitchen cabinet and is labeled in Mrs. Donat’s handwriting. This establishes that the key is a known, controlled object kept in a specific accessible domestic location, not an unknown implement. In context, it explains how the archive could be opened by someone familiar with the premises and where the key could be taken from without forced entry. When paired with the report that the key was missing by late afternoon, it supports the notion of deliberate access to the archive area on the day in question, relevant to any attempt to manage or anticipate discovery of the memorandum implicating Aldous Crane.

Clue_P1 provides Petra Hale’s account of her relationship and alibi context: she had a professional dispute with Cornelius last week over attribution for the 1847 harbour survey, which she characterizes as scholarly. She states she was at the reading-room table all afternoon and that any patron can confirm it. This frames her as having a conceivable interpersonal friction but not an evident escalation to lethal harm, and it offers a stability-of-presence claim during the likely ingestion/decline period. The clue matters primarily for narrowing suspects: it supplies an alternative motive category (professional rivalry) while also presenting an alibi-like statement that, if true, makes her less compatible with a theory requiring covert handling and delivery of poisoned tea.

Cornelius Fitch discovered Aldous Crane’s unauthorised trust transfers and wrote he would confront Crane that day and report to the magistrate that evening, giving Crane an immediate motive to stop him. Crane then admitted he had arsenic and put it in the tea. The head wound is explained by collapse, not assault. Bram, Donat, and Petra lack comparable motive and direct poison delivery linkage.
